title: Composite Indexes and Column Order
learningObjectives: Define a composite index and explain why column order matters.
Describe the leftmost-prefix principle for a composite index.
Create a multi-column index for a common query pattern.
Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to inspect a composite-index lookup.
Choose index column order based on actual filters and sorting needs.

understand.concept: A composite index contains more than one column. In SQLite, the leftmost columns of the index are especially important: a query that constrains the leading column or a leading prefix can often use the index, while a query that filters only a later column may not benefit in the same way.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing the right column order helps indexes support common multi-column filters and sort patterns without creating unnecessary indexes.
understand.analogy: An index is like a sorted lookup guide that points toward the relevant records instead of requiring every page to be read.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model B-tree pages, query planner estimates, index maintenance or the full range of SQL access paths.

explain.narrative:
## Composite indexes
A composite index stores a key made from multiple columns. For an index on (region, status), region is the leftmost column and status follows it. Queries that constrain region, or region and status together, can often use the index.

## Column order
Put columns in an order that matches real query patterns. Equality filters, range filters and ORDER BY requirements affect the best design. Do not assume an index on (a,b) is equivalent to an index on (b,a).

## Verify with query plans
Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to inspect whether the composite index is used. The exact plan text can vary, so verify the plan and the result rows.

### Leftmost-prefix reasoning
An index on `(region, status)` can generally support lookups beginning with region, including region alone or region plus status. It is not equivalent to an index on `(status, region)` for all query patterns. A query filtering only on status may not efficiently use the first index key.

### Equality and range columns
A common starting design places frequently constrained equality columns before range columns, but workload, sort requirements and selectivity matter. Confirm the actual access plan and avoid adding indexes for hypothetical queries.

examples.title: Create regional order data
examples.code: CREATE TABLE perf15_region_orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, amount INTEGER NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates a regional orders table with region, status and amount attributes. The query patterns in this lesson filter by both region and status.

examples.title: Insert sample regional orders
examples.explanation: Inserts six rows across East, West and North. Two East orders are paid, with amounts 100 and 70, giving a known total of 170.

examples.title: Create a composite index
examples.code: CREATE INDEX idx_perf15_region_status ON perf15_region_orders(region, status);
examples.explanation: Creates a composite index whose leftmost key is region and whose second key is status. The order of these columns is part of the index design, not just a cosmetic choice.

examples.title: Inspect a query that constrains both indexed columns
examples.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT order_id, amount FROM perf15_region_orders WHERE region = 'East' AND status = 'paid';
examples.explanation: Displays the access plan for a query that constrains both indexed columns with equality predicates. SQLite can use the composite index to narrow the search; exact plan wording can vary with engine version and statistics.

examples.title: Return matching rows and total
examples.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS matching_orders, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM perf15_region_orders WHERE region = 'East' AND status = 'paid';
examples.explanation: Counts the two matching paid East orders and sums their amount to 170. The result confirms the filter logic independently of whether the planner chooses the index.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and inspect the composite index plan. Identify the leading column and explain why both filters match the index key.
practise.independentTask: Create an orders table with customer, status and order_date. Design a composite index for a realistic filter and justify the column order using the queries your application runs.
